title: The Salem Witch Trials: How a Town Turned on Itself
youtube_title: The Salem Witch Trials: How a Town Turned on Itself | Full Documentary
description:
In 1692, a few girls in a Massachusetts village began having fits, and within months more than two hundred people had been accused of witchcraft. Nineteen were hanged, one old man was pressed to death with stones, and more died in jail. This is the true, fact-checked story of how fear, faith and a village feud turned neighbors against each other.

beats.say: September 1692. In a field beside the jail in Salem, an old farmer lies on his back.
Men are laying heavy stones on his chest.
The court wants one thing from him. A plea. Guilty, or not guilty.
He will not give it.
Three days later, a cart carries eight more people to a rocky ledge outside town. All eight are hanged as witches.
None of them was a witch. And the people who sent them there were their own neighbors.
Before it was over, at least twenty-five people would be dead.
This is the story of how a town turned on itself.
To understand Salem, you have to start in England.
In 1630, a fleet of eleven ships carried somewhere between seven hundred and a thousand Puritans across the Atlantic.
Many came from eastern England. Some came from a market town called Boston, and they gave its name to their new capital.
They wanted to build a godly community. A city on a hill.
And they carried with them a belief almost everyone in Europe shared. The Devil was real. And he worked through witches.
For more than a century, Europe had been hunting them.
Around Trier, in the 1580s and 1590s, hundreds were put to death.
In Würzburg and Bamberg, in the 1620s and early 1630s, nearly two thousand more.
Historians estimate that tens of thousands of people were executed across Europe.
England had its own terror in the 1640s, while the country was torn apart by civil war.
With the courts in chaos, local officials let witch-hunters work almost unchecked.
The most notorious was a man named Matthew Hopkins, who called himself the Witchfinder General. Parliament never gave him that title.
In East Anglia, in just a few years, at least a hundred people were hanged.
That was the world the New England Puritans came from.
By 1692, Salem was really two places. Salem Town was a busy port, rich from the sea.
A few miles inland lay Salem Village. Farms, fields, and a small meetinghouse.
The village wanted its own church and its own say. The town kept a firm grip.
Inside the village, families split into rival camps. Historians often point to two: the Putnams, farmers rooted in the village, and the Porters, tied to the trade of the town.
In 1689, the village hired a new minister, Samuel Parris. He had once been a merchant in Barbados.
Parris was stern, and he quarreled over his pay. Soon some villagers wanted him gone.
Then, in the dead of winter, something happened inside his own house.
January 1692. Snow lay deep around Salem Village.
In the parsonage, the minister's daughter, Betty Parris, began to have fits. She was nine years old.
Her cousin Abigail Williams, who lived with them, was eleven. Soon she was having fits too.
Witnesses said the girls screamed, twisted into strange positions, and cried out that they were being pinched and pricked.
Weeks of prayer did nothing. A doctor, most likely a local physician named William Griggs, gave his opinion. The girls were bewitched.
A neighbor, Mary Sibley, suggested an old folk remedy. A witch cake.
Two people enslaved in the Parris household, Tituba and a man called John Indian, baked it from rye meal and the girls' urine, then fed it to a dog.
It was meant to reveal who was hurting the girls. Instead, it made things worse.
More girls began to suffer. Among them was twelve-year-old Ann Putnam.
On February 29, pressed by adults to name their tormentors, the girls named three women.
Sarah Good, a poor woman who begged door to door. Sarah Osborne, an elderly woman who rarely came to church.
And Tituba herself. The records call her an Indian woman. She probably came to New England from Barbados with Parris, but her origins are still debated.
On March 1, the three were questioned in the village meetinghouse, packed with spectators.
Sarah Good and Sarah Osborne denied everything.
Tituba, under heavy pressure, confessed. She described the Devil, strange creatures, and a book signed by witches.
Why did the girls behave this way? In 1976, one researcher suggested poisoned rye, a fungus called ergot.
It is still only a hypothesis, and most historians reject it. Fear, faith, and village politics explain far more.
Because Tituba had said one more thing. There were other witches in Salem. And she did not know all their names.
The hunt was on.
And the accusers had a weapon no one could argue with. Spectral evidence.
A girl would say that a person's spirit, their specter, had come to her in the night and hurt her.
The accused could be miles away, asleep in bed. It did not matter. Only the victim could see the specter.
How do you prove your spirit was not somewhere?
Soon the accusations reached people nobody would have suspected.
Martha Corey, a church member, was arrested in March. So was Rebecca Nurse, seventy-one years old and known for her piety.
Dozens of her neighbors signed a petition swearing to her good character. It did not save her.
Rebecca had two sisters. One of them was Mary Easty, a farmer's wife from nearby Topsfield, in her late fifties.
She was arrested in April.
During her questioning, Mary clasped her hands. One of the afflicted girls, Mercy Lewis, copied her, and cried out that her own hands were stuck together.
Still, in May, for reasons the records do not explain, Mary Easty was released.
She had two days at home. Then Mercy Lewis fell into violent fits and said Mary's specter was killing her.
That night, a second warrant was issued. Mary was taken from her family and sent back to jail.
The jails were filling fast.
Prisoners were kept in chains. They or their families had to pay for their own food and keep.
Sarah Good's small daughter, Dorothy, just four or five years old, was locked up too.
Sarah Osborne never saw a trial. She died in a Boston jail in May.
By the end, more than two hundred people would be accused.
But all through the spring, there was no court to try them. That was about to change.
In May 1692, a new governor, Sir William Phips, arrived in Boston with a new royal charter.
He found the jails crowded with accused witches.
On May 27, he created a special court to deal with them. The Court of Oyer and Terminer. To hear, and to decide.
Its chief justice was William Stoughton. Samuel Sewall, a Boston merchant, was one of the judges.
The court would accept spectral evidence.
The first to be tried was Bridget Bishop, a woman who had been accused of witchcraft years before.
On June 10, she was hanged. The first to die.
One of the judges, Nathaniel Saltonstall, left the court soon after, reportedly unhappy with how the case was handled.
Days later, a group of Boston ministers warned the court to be careful with spectral evidence. The Devil, they said, could take the shape of an innocent person.
But the same letter also urged a speedy and vigorous prosecution. The court went on.
On July 19, five more women were hanged. One was Rebecca Nurse.
At her trial, the jury had first found her not guilty.
The afflicted girls erupted in fits. The chief justice asked the jury to think again. They came back with guilty.
On August 19, five more were hanged.
Among them was George Burroughs, a former minister of Salem Village itself.
On the gallows, witnesses said, he recited the Lord's Prayer without a single mistake. Many believed a witch could not do that.
The crowd stirred. According to a later account by the Boston merchant Robert Calef, the minister Cotton Mather, on horseback, calmed them, and the hanging went ahead.
We now know where these hangings took place. In 2016, researchers confirmed the site: a rocky outcrop called Proctor's Ledge.
By September, the court was moving faster than ever. And one old man was about to defy it.
Giles Corey was a farmer, about eighty years old. Tough, stubborn, and no stranger to a quarrel.
When his wife Martha was accused in March, Giles gave statements about her odd behavior. They were used against her.
Then, in April, the accusers turned on Giles himself.
He was jailed for months. When he was finally brought before the court in September, he refused to plead.
Under English law, a trial could not begin without a plea.
The answer was an old and brutal practice. The prisoner was laid down, and weights were piled on him until he answered, or died.
Giles Corey was taken to a field near the Salem jail.
Judge Samuel Sewall wrote in his diary that the court, and an old friend, spent two days trying to change his mind. All in vain.
The tradition says that each time they asked him to plead, he answered with two words. More weight.
But nobody wrote those words down in 1692. They were only recorded long afterward, and no one can be sure he said them.

show.text: About noon, at Salem, Giles Corey was press'd to death for standing mute.

beats.say: What is certain is how Sewall's diary ended the story.
Why did he do it? No one knows.
Some say he wanted to protect his land for his family. Others say he simply would not give the court what it wanted.
Three days later, on September 22, his wife Martha was hanged.
She was one of eight that day. Mary Easty was another.
Before she died, Mary wrote to the judges. She did not beg for her own life.

show.text: I petition to your honours not for my own life, for I know I must die... but that, if it be possible, no more innocent blood be shed.

beats.say: She asked them to stop.

show.label: THE DEAD OF 1692
show.sub: Hanged. Plus Giles Corey, and at least five who died in jail.

beats.say: Nineteen people had now been hanged. Not one of them was burned. That is a myth.
They were the last hangings in Salem. But no one knew that yet.
By autumn, doubt was spreading.
Accusations had reached respected families, and reportedly even the governor's own wife.
In October, the minister Increase Mather, Cotton Mather's father, published a book attacking spectral evidence.

show.text: It were better that ten suspected witches should escape, than that one innocent person should be condemned.

beats.say: It contained a line that still echoes today.
At the end of October, Governor Phips shut down the special court.
A new court took over in 1693, and spectral evidence no longer counted.
Of fifty-six people it indicted, only three were convicted. The governor pardoned them, and by May, the prisoners were set free.
Some stayed in jail even after they were cleared, until someone paid their fees.
Families had lost land, animals and savings. Within a few years, Samuel Parris was forced out of the village.
Then came the reckoning.
In January 1697, the colony held a day of fasting and prayer for what had happened.
In a Boston church, Samuel Sewall stood while his minister read out a confession on his behalf.

show.text: ...to take the blame and shame of it, asking pardon of men.

beats.say: He was the only judge to apologize in public.
Twelve of the jurors also signed an apology.
And in 1706, the girl who had accused so many, Ann Putnam, now grown up, stood in the Salem Village church while her confession was read.

show.text: It was a great delusion of Satan that deceived me in that sad time.

beats.say: She said she had been deceived.
In 1711, the colony reversed the convictions of most of the victims and paid their families nearly six hundred pounds.
It was not the end. Some names were left out for centuries.

show.label: CLEARED IN 2022
show.sub: Elizabeth Johnson Jr., the last to be exonerated

beats.say: The very last was Elizabeth Johnson Junior, condemned in 1693 but never executed.
In 2022, after an eighth-grade class took up her cause, Massachusetts finally cleared her name.
Salem Village no longer exists by that name. Today it is the town of Danvers.
But the lesson it left is still with us. When fear becomes evidence, anyone can be guilty.
